speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
When this House adjourns on Friday March 26th instant, it stand adjourned until Tuesday April 6th next.
He said: Before the motion is put, may I say to hon. members of the House that the government has no intention of pressing this motion, unless it meets with approval on the part of hon. members. The motion has been made because the government has reason to believe that to most of the members it would be a convenience to have an adjoum-

ment of ten days, which we would have if this motion carries, rather than to be obliged to come back for two days and one-half during that period of time, thereby breaking the adjournment of ten continuous days which would otherwise be possible. The custom has been to adjourn on the Wednesday afternoon before Easter, the House sitting for half a day on Wednesday, and then adjourning until the following Tuesday. I have had occasion to look up the record and I find that in the years 1917 to 1925 the practice has been to adjourn on the Wednesday. Monday and Tuesday are full days and Wednesday half a day. If this motion does not carry, members will be obliged to come back for two days and a half the following week. If the motion carries it will be possible for hon. members to leave the city on Friday night of this week and remain away until Tuesday of the week after next. The government, in view of what has been communicated to its members, has thought that, with that feature drawn to the attention of hon. members, the motion would probably meet with general approval. However, the purpose of presenting the motion at the moment is rather to call forth an expression of the views of hon. members, and if the views of hon. members appear to be against the motion, I would ask that it stand.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As far as I am individually concerned, and as far as my own convenience goes, the motion would suit me very well, but the members on this side of the House, especially those from the far west and far east, are, if I may be permitted to speak their minds as indicated to me, strongly against this motion. Their reasons are chiefly their anxiety to get on with the business of the session, and added to that there is the fact that the business of the House seems to be a joke to hon. members opposite. There is also the fact that we have just had quite a long recess of about ten or eleven days during which most of the members, I think, availed themselves of the opportunity of returning home, and naturally they do not feel like inviting another opportunity to go back home, spending most of the time, as is necessary, on the way. For these two reasons, the feeling on this side of the House would be against the motion, and I would suggest that, if it is not dropped, it stand, until perhaps a further conference could be had.

Personally I would prefer to have the adjournment. It seems to me that out of the ten days there would be only two and1 one-half

Easter Adjournment
days during which we could really be doing any work in the House. I would like to have gone west. If there is any strenuous opposition to the longer adjournment, I am quite willing to bow to the will of the majority, but we would only lose two and one-half working days out of the ten days. The adjournment would be broken by Saturday and Sunday, the legal holidays intervening, and it would 'be only two and one-half days longer than the regular adjournment. During that period there are, of course, five legal holidays. It seems to me it would be to the convenience of all hon. members to have the adjournment for ten days. I think the government have had adjournment enough. They have had two weeks. I have had to remain in Ottawa as have a great many other hon. members. At the same time if there is anything to be gained by it I would be in favour of the longer adjournment. Seeing that only two and one-half days during which we could do any business would be lost, I think hon. members would be well advised to vote for the ten day adjournment. I am quite willing to stay here or I am quite willing to go home.

This is an occasion when I wish to say a word or two. I was not able to return to Vancouver during the previous adjournment. I think the public at large and members generally are anxious to get on with the business of the country, for there is a good deal to be done. I myself have a copyright bill which I should like to proceed with and I would urge upon the government the wisdom, even if we have only two and a half days, to let us use all our time in getting some work done. It might mean some personal inconvenience to hon. gentlemen who would like to return to their homes, but that should not stand in the way of public business.
Mr. HARRY J. BARBER (Fraser Valley): As one who took advantage of the last adjournment I may say that I spent ten days in travelling, having only two days at home. To hon. gentlemen in the far west and east who could not avail themselves of the adjournment it would mean much inconvenience: they would have to remain in Ottawa until the re-assembling of parliament. I think that those hon. members from Ontario and Quebec, who have easy access to their homes, should have some consideration for others who come from a distance. We are anxious to proceed with the business of the country, and we hope to make the session as short as possible. We are looking forward to the other end of the session, and we would
rather work now. I for one am very much opposed to a further adjournment.

The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has asked for an expression of opinion regarding the duration of the adjournment at Easter. My right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) has represented the views held by many hon. members sitting on this side of the House, and personally I would wish to emphasize this point, that this is a longer Easter vacation than usual. Let us bear in mind the previous adjournment of eleven or twelve days which we had very recently. In the light of that vacation I submit that the proposed adjournment should be as short as possible, rather than one which will be longer than any we have had in the last five or six years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As I intimated a moment ago, it is not the desire of the government to press the motion at all. If I act on the suggestion which has been made to allow it to stand until Thursday, the whips might confer among themselves in the meantime. Let me make it clear that the government is as anxious as any hon. member on the opposite side to proceed with the business of parliament, but we have felt that in matters relating to the procedure of the House there may be occasions when mutual accommodation would also help to expedite business. As to what my hon. friend has just said about the proposed adjournment being longer than usual at Easter, he will recall that parliament assembled this year earlier than is customary. The House met early in the month of January, and for that reason the period of time during which hon. members have already been away from their homes is longer than is usual at Easter. However, it is a matter of meeting the convenience of the majority of members.

Speaking from the standpoint of the convenience of members, it seems to me that, whatever is going to be done, the sooner we know what is decided upon, the better, in order that we may be enabled to make our arrangements. If the Prime Minister would permit me to interview the whips of the Liberal and Progressive parties this afternoon, we might come to some understanding and we could know the decision to-night. It would inconvenience hon. members greatly to be obliged to wait until Thursday or Friday to know what the government intended doing.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

I rise to a question of privilege. Last night, at the conclusion of the speech of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), I rose to call the attention of the House to a certain statement that had been made with reference to myself earlier in the day by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), in which he misquoted a speech which I had delivered in Toronto. The hon. member referred to certain remarks of mine as rightly quoted by the non. the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) at page 67 of Hansard of the present session, and further put into my mouth these words:
Had we had autonomy we should not have entered the war. I
I never used these words. I have nothing to retract from what I said on that occasion but inasmuch as the hon. member omitted the qualifying text of my speech I desire to quote rather extensively from a report of it. Parenthetically, I may observe, Mr. Speaker, that I would not have risen on this occasion were it not that I was prevented last night from making the explanation when I had a perfect right to do so in view of the fact that I had the floor beyond any dispute. The hon. member for Labelle had moved an amendment which was not seconded, and which it appears was not in proper shape, and he had gone to the clerk's table to have it redrafted as I presume and went around looking for a seconder. I therefore had the floor and I was prepared to make the present explanation then. What the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said was not altogether correct. He quoted only one sentence and at that not as to the text. I should like to read the following extract from the speech I gave at Toronto in order to make my position clear. I quote:
I am opposed to separatism, changing Canada's status and autonomy. We are proud that Canada is an integral part of the greatest empire the world has ever known. The war has not changed Canada's status. What She has done in the past thirty-five years she has done of her own free will and voluntarily 
Canadians have good reason to know that the national status of Canada was a good enough status for more than 400,000 Canadian soldiers to fight for. Canada's present national status in 1914 was a good enough national status for over 50,000 Canadians to die for. That status was good enough for fighting Canadians like the Canadians of St. Julien, The Orchard, Cour-cellette, Vimy Ridge, Passchendaele and many another field of battle. That status should be good enough for talking Canadians and writing Canadians. The British Empire and the British navy are our friends. The socialists who would wreck the British Empire and the pacifist who would weaken the British navy are our enemies.
I stand on the platform of our late beloved leader, Sir John A. Macdonald, when he said: A British subject I was born, a British subject I will die and I will never see General Election become commander-in-chief of the British forces or take the place of the British fleet to protect our shores. I have more faith in the sentiment expressed by the writer of "Ye mariners of England" and all it stands for than I have in the Monroe doctrine, the League of Nations, or any other similar debating society to safeguard Canada's shores in the future should trouble ever come again, which God forbid.
Canada is not going to be talked out of the British empire, if it could be done, the hon. member from
Labelle and the two gentlemen who call themselves the so called labour party-the whole party and nothing but the party would have accomplished this feat long ago. They are but a vest pocket edition of J. Ramsay MacDonald and his ideals. "Something has been said about holding elections and going to the country for endorsation before sending troops from Canada to participate in Britain's wars. So far as the Toronto sixteen regiments and units are concerned, no legislation nor no election nor no conscription act will be necessary. They will do their duty for the Empire as each separate exigency occurs the same as they have always done in the past."
This and the quotation appearing at page 67 of Hansard is what I said. I am glad to have had this opportunity of explaining my position in the matter.

speechtext: The House resumed from March 10 consideration in committee of the resolution of Hon. Mr. Robb respecting the Canada-West Indies trade agreement, Mr. Duff in the chair.

As the agreement in question is of very considerable interest to the city of Montreal, whose board of trade have taken a great deal of pains to consider that matter, I would like to place before the committee one or two considerations. In dealing with a trade convention with the West India islands, I am not speaking without some knowledge and experience of the conditions there. I have lived in British Guiana on several occasions for many months at a time; I have been on the islands of Trinidad and Tobago on several occasions for months at a time, and I have also been to a number of the other islands, for the purpose of investigating financial and trade conditions and commercial possibilities there for certain clients. Therefore, I personally feel disposed to make every reasonable concession on the part of Canada in order to improve our trade relations with those people, colonies of Great Britain, who are like ourselves under the British crown. Personally I do not think this convention will secure for Canada a very much larger trade with the West Indies than we have enjoyed under the convention of June 1920. Nevertheless, as the government have entered into that convention, there are strong considerations why we should approve of it if it is at all possible, in the public interest, to do so.
It seems to me that at this stage the government are bound, before we are called upon to approve of that convention, to state very clearly to the House what it will cost Canada. In respect of the convention of June 1920, which called for services both to the eastern and to the western groups of islands, we are told by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) that it was found impossible for Canada to

live up to that agreement. Now when a new convention is negotiated we should know definitely whether Canada can live up to this second substituted agreement, and what it will cost the treasury of Canada if we do live up to it.
In respect of the first convention of 1920 the government must have on file complete statements of what the cost of that service would have been if it had been carried out as originally intended. This House should be fully informed of what that cost would have been; how high the cost was, and what were the insuperable difficulties in the way of the government carrying it out since they came into office in 1921. We agreed under the 1920 convention to give to the eastern group of islands, a steamship service consisting of a weekly mail, passenger and freight service, and we gave instead a fortnightly mail, passenger and freight service by subsidizing the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company. On each alternate week we gave a service restricted to freight through the medium of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. As to the western group, we agreed to give a fortnightly freight, mail and passenger service to the Bahamas, Jamaica and British Honduras. We did furnish a service every third instead of every second week, and provided no cold storage, as had been in contemplation. We now agree to give not a service once every three weeks, but a fortnightly passenger, mail and freight service consisting of larger and faster steamships, and therefore a more expensive service by far than was proposed in 1920. We also now propose to give on alternative weeks a fortnightly freight service with cold storage, with a subsidiary line for freight sailing from Jamaica to Honduras every two weeks. Therefore there is no doubt in my mind that the proposed service to the western group of islands under the convention now before the committee will prove a far more expensive service than that proposed in 1920, which the government, in the interests of the country, found it impossible to carry out.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Is there not also this
difference, which I think should be interjected, that the cold storage service guaranteed in 1920 was only as business warranted, whereas now it is absolute?

Quite so. The service
from 1921 to 1925, performed to the extent which I have noted, has, I understand, proved very unprofitable indeed, and this is true with respect to the present time and recent months. I am informed, and I think quite reliably in-

Canada-West Indies Agreement
formed, that only 40 per cent or 50 per cent of the cargo space of the steamships employed at these infrequent intervals has been taken up. Therefore the new service which is proposed depends to a large extent, it seems to me, upon the successful prosecution of the banana trade with Jamaica.
When this convention was being negotiated the council of the Montreal Board1 of Trade wrote a letter, through their secretary, to the then Minister of Trade and Commerce, Hon. Thomas A. Low, in which they set out that all the people in Canada engaged in commerce are very desirous of having improved reciprocal trade relationships with the West Indies. But they state, under date of June 16, 1925::
. With regard to the suggestion that the Canadian government should build new ships for the West Indies service, the council would strongly oppose any such scheme at the present time, believing that the existing trade conditions and the enormous burden of debt under which Canada is suffering, together with its already serious transportation problems, render exceedingly ill-advised the expenditure of any considerable sum of public money on a project, the profits from which are at least problematical.
I might be allowed to say, with all deference to the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm), who discussed this question the other day, that undoubtedly the West Indies were represented by very able and experienced men. I have had many years experience with the officials of those governments, and a few years ago, but not now, I knew nearly every prominent merchant in those islands. They are very able and experienced men, and they came to that convention, undoubtedly, knowing exactly what they wished to obtain, and they were dealing with men who very largely were ignorant of the conditions in those islands, and not sufficiently informed, I think, to deal with the matter so as to protect to the utmost possible extent the interests of the treasury of Canada. But, we are told by the hon. member for North Bruce, the representatives of the government acted very largely upon the advice of those West Indian representatives, and in reading the report of those negotiations I find that those gentlemen from the West Indies dealt very frankly with the representatives of the government, and they did not pretend that any very large increase in the exportations of Canada to the West Indies was likely to be obtained under the convention which they then .proposed. However, after this latter convention was negotiated, the council of the Montreal Board of Trade passed this resolution, which I understand was also brought to the notice of the government. I quote: The council regrets that the negotiators of the agreement did not accept its suggestions concerning the

steamship services, and fears that the heavy commitments on this account may provoke such opposition as to render it impossible for parliament to sanction an agreement which includes provisions of some value to the trade between this country and those other portions of the empire which are parties to it.
More recently I am informed that the board of trade, under date of March 3rd, received from its own sub-committee which was investigating the prospects of trade under this new agreement a report, in which it is stated:
That, in respect of the commitments on account of steamship services, the agreement far exceeds the recommendations made by your predecessor-
That is the predecessor committee of the board of trade:
-and in the opinion of your committee it is unlikely that the increased trade which will result from the very considerable extension of the mutual preferences provided by the agreement will, at any rate for some years, warrant the heavy cost of the in ip roved steamship services proposed;
That, notwithstanding the financial burden undertaken by Canada as referred to in the foregoing paragraph, your committee is strongly of opinion that, considering the serious effects upon the West Indies and other colonies concerned and upon the trade relations of the empire, of a failure on the part of Canada to ratify the agreement negotiated in good faith by the duly accredited representatives of all the parties thereto, the said agreement should be approved by parliament without delay;
That, in thus urging the approval of the agreement, your committee does not recede from its former objection to the building of vessels by the Canadian government, being still unalterably opposed to any extension of government ownership or operation of steamships, but it hopes that the provision of the additional steamship services necessary may be secured by means of subsidies to private lines, thus minimizing the burden on the heavily taxed citizens of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I do not concede personally that parliament is bound to ratify this convention simiply because the representatives of the West India islands have in good faith negotiated the convention, always subject to the approval of their own councils and legislatures and subject to the approval of the Canadian parliament, but, on the other hand, I do admit that the government of Canada having negotiated the convention, no slight objection on the part either of this House or of the country should defeat the confirmation and approval of that treaty if the costs of the services to be provided are at all commensurate with the advantages which Canada would receive by putting the treaty and the auxiliary steamship services into operation during the term of the treaty, the next twelve years.
I quite appreciate that dealing with the representative men of the West Indies, it is desirable that we should support the government's action in negotiating the treaty if it is at all practicable for us to do so. becaus?

Canada-West Indies Agreement
on the part of Canada I personally would rather see some financial sacrifice than to disclose to them by the vote of this committee and of this House that the government which negotiated this treaty did it through incompetent officers andi representatives, and negotiated it without having first carefully ascertained what the cost would be to the public treasury of Canada.
On the 8th of March of the present year the council of the Montreal Board of Trade placed their final views before the right hon. leader of this government in a letter written by the secretary of the board, in which they say:
I have the honour to communicate the views of the council of this board on the question of the ratification by the Canadian parliament of the Canada-West Indies Trade Agreement, 1925, as follows:
On 16th June, 1925, just prior to the meeting of representatives of the Dominion and of the West Indies and other colonies interested, at which the agreement was drawn up, the council of this board submitted to the hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce certain recommendations with regard to provisions which in its opinion should be embodied in that agreement. These recommendations included one to the effect that this country should go to the utmost possible limit in the granting of reductions in its tariff in favour of the West Indies, as well as very definite suggestions as to the necessity of keeping the expenditure on steamship services at the lowest possible minimum, and above all the council voiced its strong opposition to any proposal that the Canadian government should build new ships for this service, pointing out that the enormous burden c<f debt under which Canada is now suffering, together with its already serious transportation problems, render exceedingly ill-advised the expenditure of any considerable sum of public money on such a project.
To the great regret of the council the agreement as negotiated involves very heavy commitments on account cf steamship services.
While still unalterably opposed to any extension of government ownership or operation of steamships, the council nevertheless believes that failure on the part of Canada to ratify the West Indies agreement, negotiated in good faith by the duly accredited representatives of all the part es thereto, and since ratified by all those parties with the exception of this Dominion, would have the most serious consequences, and it therefore urges the ratification of the agreement by parliament without, delay.
The council cannot refrain from expressing the hope that the government may find it possible to secure the necessary additional steamship services by means of subsidies to private lines, rather than by launching into an expensive programme of shipbuilding, believing that thereby the additions to the financial burden on the already heavily taxed citizens of this Dominion would be minimized.
Now it is all very well for the council of the Montreal Board of Trade to submit the opinion that under the circumstances, in order to maintain the good reputation of the government of Canada with those with whom it negotiated this convention, we should endorse the expenditure of untold thousands, yes of millions, without having before it definite details as to that cost. Although I

concede to no man, to no member of this committee, a stronger desire to maintain friendly and profitable commercial relations with the West India islands, yet I do not feel that as a representative, even of the city of Montreal, I should vote blindly in favour of the approval and confirmation of this later convention, unless we have from the Minister of Finance, or from the Prime Minister, or from some other of his ministry-the Minister of Trade and Commerce for instance- a clear and precise statement of what in their opinion, backed up by the best information which they can obtain, the carrying out of this convention will cost the country for the next twelve years. I have seen, and have at hand, a report of a committee of the Board of Trade of Halifax in reference to this matter. [DOT] I know well the gentlemen who are on that committee. I know that they are competent business men who have had a large and varied experience in steamship matters, and especially in the matter of trade with the West India islands. Their good faith in making the calculation which they do cannot be questioned by anyone in view of their standing in the commercial community, and they estimate that the capital expenditure alone upon this steamship service may reach a total of $9,550,000 if the government undertakes to buy the ships and to operate them as a part of its mercantile marine. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that it is due to this committee, and to the House, and to the country, that the government should give us a complete statement of its policy

whether it intends to enter upon this large capital expenditure, or whether it intends to subsidize independent steamship companies to carry out these services. I quite appreciate the remark made by the hon. Minister of Finance the other day, that in view of the fact that tenders have been asked for it would be inexpedient on the part of the government to make an announcement as to what its definite policy was, or as to what the proposed cost of the services would be, until such time as these tenders may be received. But, Mr. Chairman, the delay in asking for tenders in respect of a convention made in June, 1925, is not due to any member on this side of the House. It is due to the undoubted fact that the members of the government have been much engaged since June, 1928, in their political propaganda leading up to the general elections of October 29, last, and since that day they have been deprived of their political and intellectual head and of his

Canada-West Indies Agreement
direction in the matter. We are not responsible for that, and before you ask us, as intelligent and honest members of this committee and of this House, to approve of a convention which may entail this enormous expenditure of money we are entitled to have the full facts placed before us; and if, owing to the fact that tenders are still being called for, the government does not feel in the position now to give us that information, certainly it should postpone, or be willing to postpone, the further definite consideration of this convention until after the Easter holidays when the tenders in question will have been received.
Personally I desire to suport the convention if I possibly can, but I am not going to support it at a cost of $9,500,000 of capital expenditure to this country. IVe desire full information too, because other matters of very considerable importance are to be brought before this House involving very large appropriations of public money, and tl for one am not going to oppose large grants from the public treasury to the west and to the centre of Canada, and then turn round and vote for equally large or larger appropriations for services which are less valuable to the country, simply because the city of Montreal may be interested therein. As an honest and, I think, fairly intelligent representative 'I want to have the full facts stated to us so that there may be no deception-I am not saying that in an unpleasant way

so far as we are concerned.
We must be fully informed and 4 p,m. be in a position to vote intelligently on this matter. I put it to the Minister of Finance, who has a reputation to sustain as a competent and experienced business man if he would submit to any board of any corporation, of which he may be a director and official, an agreement of such a character and ask them to take it blindly without knowing, with a very considerable degree of definiteness, the actual expenditures that would be involved in the corporation carrying out such a project. He could not maintain his reputation as a competent business man by so doing. Therefore, I think that as we are to have some sort of an adjournment during the coming Easter holidays this matter should be deferred until the committee and the House may be fully informed as to the extent of the financial obligations they are undertaking by approving this convention, and may be able to determine each member for himself whether, having regard to our sentimental interest in the West India
islands, our sentimental and political desire to co-operate with them effectually and fully and at the same time conserve the interests of this country, we are justified in voting the very large amount from the public treasury of Canada which the present convention will undoubtedly entail.

I wish to take this opportunity of referring somewhat briefly to the matter under discussion, the Canada-West Indies agreement. Many of us have followed the discussions in the House during the last five years, and several of us have taken part in those discussions. Whether one approves of the present treaty or whether one disapproves, I believe all are in accord on this point: that there is great need of an improved service of ships between Canada and the West Indies, a better modern class of boats, better passenger accommodation, better facilities for freight and for cold storage. There is another point on which I believe we will all agree, and that is that it is necessary to observe the fulfilment of the treaty between the West Indies and ourselves. A very decided complaint has been made regarding the method in which Canada has performed its obligations under the treaty. I believe it is correct to say that it is necessary to maintain at, least, the conditions at present, or there must be some other change. I present these two points; a better transportation service in many respects and a fulfilment of the conditions that have been laid down in the present act, or as may be promised in the proposed act. Then there is the third point, and surely we will agree upon that; that it is necessary for us to move on and search out to increase our trade with the West Indies. Whether the future is a great one, or whether it is not so great the fact is there is much left for Canada to do in increasing the West Indian trade so that these are the three main features on which I believe the members of this House all agree.
Let me say a word on a few points arising in this discussion. I think there is some misapprehension amongst some hon. members of this House as to the terms of the present treaty or agreement. First of all, let me say that to-day all imports coming from the West Indies to Canada can pass through the United States on the same terms as if they were entering Canada directly. It is true there is a provision that on six months' notice Canada may insist or may require that imports come direct to Canada, but that provision is not enforced and never has been enforced Many members in this House will remember that this matter has been pressed on the government for several years, and a feature of this

Canada-West Indies Agreement
agreement that one must recognize with satisfaction is that the government has incorporated in it and propose to enforce the requirement that all imports from the West Indies come direct to Canada. That is one of the favourable features of the treaty. Another point I wish to make is, that with reference to the imports from the West Indies at the present time, the statistics do not represent accurately, or even fairly, the amount of business we do with the West Indies. Most strikingly is this true with regard to bananas. At the present time a large quantity of the bananas imported into Canada is obtained through the United States. They may be West India bananas and they may not, but they are credited as an import from the United States. The United States ' does not grow bananas, but in the method of compiling customs statistics the import is credited to the United States, because our bananas are purchased and paid for there. I point this out because all bananas, whatever the amount may be, that are got from the United States, to almost the entire extent, appear as imports from that country, whereas, really they may be indirectly imports from the West Indies. Then there is the further point that under the preference provided for, it is reasonable to expect that a large part of the import of bananas will come from the West Indies direct. To that extent the benefit of a treaty with the West Indies, will be apparent because instead of importing through the United States, we can reasonably look for a very considerable increased importation through our Canadian ports.
Let me refer to the question of the quantity of bananas, because one may reasonably ask. can Jamaica, which is the principal island for the growth of this fruit, supply Canada with bananas? To give an illustration of the enormous amount of this fruit that is imported into the United States, let me say that in the year 1924, 47,000,000 bunches were imported into that country. In 1924 Canada imported 2,000,000 bunches from the United States, to the value of $4,500,000. From the British West Indies direct we imported only 7,000 bunches at a value of $14,000, a marked contrast between the imports of bananas from the West Indies and the imports from the United States. In 1924, Jamaica exported a total of almost 12,000,000 bunches Of bananas. Our requirements were about 2,000,000. It is therefore clear that there is ample production of bananas in the West Indies to supply Canada, but it is not clear at the moment whether the bananas that come into Canada actually come from the West Indies. Some no doubt

do, others do not; there is no customs return that will decide that point. But the important factor is that they will come to Canada from the West Indies under favourable conditions, and one would hope that this trade may be added to the business that is now going on between Canada and the West Indies.
There is a further point that should give us a favourable view of our future trade with the West Indies. It is this. We know that the business that we have has grown up largely without the assistance, or at any rate, with the very limited assistance, of trade agents. We have been informed in this House that the United States have trade agents scattered all through the islands of the Caribbean sea while it is a fact that the number of Canadian agents is extraordinarily few. I would suggest to the government therefore that, whatever agreement may be arrived at in the future, the matter of trade agents should should be carefully considered and due attention paid to their employment, inasmuch as the trade must depend to a considerable extent on the work of these agents. It is encouraging, in my opinion, to reflect that the trade which we have had during the past few years has been almost independent of the activities of agent?.
There must always be a start in movements of this kind, and a start has been made in the development of our relations with the West Indies. The trade has never reached any great proportions, however. Is it not reasonable to expect that our relations with the British West Indies will lead in the future to trade with other West Indian islands that are not British, as well as with that portion of the continent which is known as Central America? These fields naturally should and I believe would, open up as the result of a well defined policy of West Indian trade.
On the other hand, consideration must be given to the adverse views held in relation to the proposed treaty with the West Indies. One must pay regard to the opinions of Canadian West Indian merchants, and we should defer to some extent to the views of the various boards of trade which are interested in the prosperity of this country. There are a number of important merchants in Canada who disapprove of conditions of the proposed treaty, and I am aware that the Halifax board of trade has pronounced strongly against its terms. I hold a copy of that board of trade's decision on this question and I have no doubt other hon. members have also received copies. A similar report was

Canada-West Indies Agreement
published two or three years ago and was concurred in by the council of the St. John Board of Trade. It is necessary to refer to these things because they must receive consideration. These reports may represent very valuable opinions.
Now what is the outstanding objection to the treaty as proposed? The objection is the enormous cost which it is said it will entail. My own personal attitude towards the treaty is a favourable one. Of course, I do not think it proper to take too optimistic a view of it, and I believe that possibly such a view was held by the late member for Cumberland, who was tremendously interested in the subject. Probably his views were too optimistic; I do not consider the West Indian trade an eldorado for Canada. At the same time there are those who hold too pessimistic a view of our future trade with the West Indies. I believe there is room for substantial growth in that trade, perhaps not to any enormous extent, but something tangible and worth while.
How can one decide in a matteT of this [DOT] kind? It is contended very forcibly that the future business between the two countries is not sufficient to warrant our going into any very heavy expenditure. We must be careful therefore in promoting this trade agreement; we must make some reservation in forming our opinions on the subject. I would suggest therefore that, before we come to a final decision in the matter, as close an estimate as possible be given to the House as to what cost will be involved in carrying the treaty into effect. I do not want to scrutinize the cost too closely, but it should not be excessive. There is however something more than a mere commercial arrangement in such a treaty. We are carrying on or we should carry on, relations with another portion of the empire, so that not only is there the commercial aspect of the treaty to be considered; there is also the national responsibility which I think we should regard. We must have further details with regard to the expense that will be entailed. It may be that later on in this debate, or when the matter comes down in the form of a bill, that information will be largely supplied.
There is one other point to which I would refer here. I notice that there is a provision giving the Canadian government power to call at any port other than those specified in the agreement. Perhaps at some stage the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) will give us the full information on that point, as to whether the treaty may include ports in the United States or elsewhere.

Mr. Chairman, I do not desire to make any general criticism of this treaty at the present time, for the reason that I am in favour of the policy of trade treaties between the sister dominions as a means of bringing them closer together in commercial relations. But I do maintain that in the framing of such treaties every care and every caution should be exercised to see to it that our commitments are not too large, and that they are in proportion to the benefits that we are to receive. In the framing of this treaty I fear the government have been misled in important matters, and all my criticism is directed against that part of the programme dealing with the importations of bananas and the banana carrying business. I believe the government have been misled in this matter and have attached altogether too much importance to the possibility of diverting to our Canadian ports the large banana carrying trade which comes to us now, almost entirely through United States ports.
I claim, Mr. Speaker, to have some knowledge of this business, and of the difficulties of transportation, refrigeration, storage and the distribution of this fruit, and I state frankly to this House that I do not believe the plan to divert this traffic to Canadian ports feasible or practical. I am not going into detail as to why that is my opinion, but if permitted I will read a few extracts from a report of the Halifax Board of Trade, dealing with this matter, which is in the possession of many hon. members.
Where then can the increased traffic to warrant the expenditures be 'expected to come from? The only remaining article suggested is /bananas and a great deal has been said about them at the conference. The agreement provides that all bananas imported direct into Canada from British .possessions shafil be entirely free of duty and that ail coming from or through a foreign country shall pay a flat duty of 50 cents per stem or bunch. For the fiscal year ending March, 1925, Canada imported 2,464,925 bundles. Of these
100.000	came to the Maritime provinces, 2,059,369 to Quebec and Ontario, 303,396 to the prairif provinces and 133 to the Yukon. The greater bulk of these-
2.118.000	bunches were imported during April to November or eight months of the year.
Presuming that the ships as proposed are provided, they could carry 240,000 bunches per month. The importation during the month of May was 317,847; June, 360,369; July, 444,154; August, 376,274, showing that during these months a considerable quantity would have still to come through the United States to satisfy the demand or more tonnage provided for
that period and during the remaining months of the year, December to March inclusive, the costly ships proposed for the service would be required to operate carrying from 70,000 to 130,000 per month with a capacity of 240,000 bunches. It is not hard to see how the operating losses would pile up during that period.
The above is based on the presumption that all the bananas used in Canada would come by the ships proposed for the western service from Jamaica to Canadian ports but this is not at all likely to occur. Owing to the perishable nature of the bananas the shortest route and quickest transportation is necessary to avoid loss by deterioration, therefore all the bananas used in western Canada and possibly some used in Ontario are brought by steamer to Mobile or New Orleans, a two or three day voyage, and shipped to destination by rail, and the rail haul is shorter than from Canadian sea ports to similar points, creating a saving of six to seven days in the sea voyage and a possibly lower railway freight; is it not reasonable to assume that the saving in freight and lesser deterioration will offset the duty of 50 cents per bunch and admit that the bananas for western Canada will continue to move that w'ay? This would leave 2,000,000 bunches to be imported direct by the proposed steamer. The first question that occurs to us is, "Who is going to operate the business?" Will the Jamaica growers or merchants form a company to load the ships, establish a selling and distributing organization in Canada and sell to the Canadian dealer on as suitable terms and conditions as they buy at present? If so, the problem would be simplified and even though by virtue of their control of the business they would probably derive the whole benefit of the duty imposed on bananas of 50 cents per bunch, when imported via the United States, the proposal would have some little merit if it increased our exports to Jamaica. But if we know the Jamaica growers and merchants that is not likely to happen-they want to sell their bananas to somebody in Jamaica for cash and take no risks of the market conditions in Canada.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I -would ask the committee to take particular note of article 13. This article deals largely with the inauguration of this service, which is to deal practically with the banana situation. It would seem to me that the entire plan is linked up with this banana business, and a large part of the cost of equipping these steamers will be devoted to that purpose. Steamer service is to be provided for storage and refrigeration for 70,000 bunches, and freight service for 50,000 bunches. The important point-and I direct the attention of the committee to it- is that if the government fail to secure this traffic, a good deal of this expenditure will have been wasted, and the revenue which they expect to receive will have been lost. I claim that before this matter is intelligently voted upon we should have some statement from the government as to just how they propose to carry on this business.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) a few questions in connection with this particular part of the treaty:
1.	What information was available in reference to this industry, when the treaty wa3 negotiated? Did they have reports from experts, or first-hand information from those
Canada-West Indies Agreement

connected with this business here in Canada, such as dealers, transportation companies or distributors?
2.	Where they fully informed as to the extremely perishable nature of this fruit and the great difficulties of distribution without heavy loss?
3.	Were they advised of the fact that less than one-third of the total imports of bananas to the United States and Canada came from the West Indies, and that these West Indies imports were desirable only at certain seasons and for certain markets?
4.	What arrangements or plans do the government propose as to the importation and distribution of this fruit? Will the government go into the importing business themselves, or have they in view some corporation or company that will take on the job?
5.	Was any information supplied dealing with previous efforts to divert this traffic by transportation companies or other corporations or individuals?
6.	Did they have any knowledge of the fact that millions of dollars have been expended by large corporations in the industry in experimental work, in growing, handling, refrigeration, transportation and distribution of this fruit, and that inspection stations are maintained at all important junctions, and a messenger service established which watches carefully the temperature of every car of bananas en route to its destination, and that the most satisfactory plan of distribution is based upon the shortest haul and quickest delivery from steamer side to centres of distribution?
I will send a copy of these questions over to the minister.

The minister admits the fact that in 1923 there was a reduction in the duty on refined sugar of one-half a cent per pound. The very next day the sugar beet growers in western Ontario- and there are tens of thousands of people interested in the production of sugar beets- had the price of their sugar beets reduced fifty cents per ton. As a result of that reduction the people in the counties adjoining the district in western Ontario where I live lost many hundreds of thousands of dollars. The minister now says that the preference will not be entered into as far as Australia is concerned until the present agreement between the West India islands and Canada becomes operative. Then, if I understand the matter correctly, as soon as the treaty with the West Indies goes into operation a similar trade arrangement between Australia and Canada will become effective. These treaties will allow the raw products of the sugar from Australia and the West Indies to enter Canada at a lower price than they have ever entered before thereby competing with the product of the growers of sugar beets in my part of the province of Ontario. Such being the case I have good reason to protest against entering into any such arrangement as the present without the minister first investigating the needs of the industry affected. I should like to ask the minister whether he really did make an investigation before bringing down this treaty in order to find out what effect it would have so far as the producers of sugar beets in Canada are concerned? Perhaps the minister would like to answer that question at a later date, but let me say to him it is a matter of vital importance to our people.
I have already drawn the attention of the government to the position of sugar refiners. The minister has already been shown that there will be a loss of revenue of
5 p.m. at least one million dollars, and that the total obligation to be shouldered by the people of Canada in connection with the investments involved here and in other matters, will reach a total of some $10,000,000. What are we to get in return for this treaty? I cannot do better than repeat the statement which was made in this connection by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Black) on Friday evening last:
The West Indies get large quantities of fish from their own waters. In that connection I should like to read this extract from the report of the conference with the West India delegates. The vice-chairman is questioning Mr. Leacock, a delegate from Barbados.
"The Vice-Chairman: Your suggestion is that the preference given now is sufficient?
"Mr. Leacock: Yes, as far as we are concerned.''

Mr. Leacock says further:
"The Vice-Chairman: Before you sit down, Mr. Leacock, do you think it well to say something about what you can give to Canada?
"Mr. Leacock: Well, that is a very difficult point of view for me to touoh upon, because, as I say, Canada has the entire flour trade with the exception of what she cannot supply; she has the entire oat trade of our colonies, the entire oatmeal trade of our colonies, et cetera. Our manufactured goods come very largely from the United Kingdom, and the only article, as it appears to me, that we could encourage in trade with Canada by an increased preference, is the item of salted meats, which could bo turned over to Canada, and would probably go over quicker if you got an increased preference. That is as far as I can see as far as Barbados is concerned."
What he says applies not only to Barbados but to all the islands of the West Indies and to Bermuda.
If that represents the total increase in trade we may expect from this treaty surely it is not worth the enormous sums of money which Canada will be compelled to pay. The minister must realize the fact that labour in the West Indies is the cheapest kind of labour in the world, that a large portion of the population in those islands,-as has been already stated here-represents the second lowest type of civilization on the face of the globe, and that it is practically impossible for us to expect to develop trade to any greater extent than is now taking place. We protect our manufacturers from cheap labour; why not protect our farmers?
I wish, further, to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that the people in my district, at any rate during the last season, in order to find a market were compelled to ship nearly 200,000 tons of sugar beets to the United States, and that those farmers making the shipment were not only compelled to pay the freight to the sugar refineries but also an excise duty of 80 cents per ton at the border before their sugar beets could obtain admission into that country. What encouragement have these farmers to build a sugar refinery in the face of treaties such as we are entering into at this session of parliament? I have called the minister's attention to the fact that in my own home town the farmers, with their organization of over four thousand members, gathered together $200,000. Our town granted them a large site and built a railway siding into the plant. They commenced to build the plant and spent over $200,000, and there it stands. But instead of those farmers receiving encouragement for the development of their industry, the minister now takes advantage of that treaty to interfere materially with the future development of the industry. When the minister reduced the duty on refined sugar by half a cent a pound, the farmers were compelled, as I said, to accept fifty cents per ton less on their sugar

Canada-West Indies Agreement
beets. If a farmer produced sixteen tons of sugar beets to the acre, he was then compelled in 1924 to accept eight dollars per acre less for his product. When these treaties go into effect, how much less will he receive, and what encouragement is there for the farmers to proceed to develop this industry? It is a basic industry of our country, one in which we should all be vitally interested. The western provinces have been able to demonstrate the fact that they can grow beets up there successfully. They have built a refinery, as I understand, and are trying to carry on, but what encouragement have these men to continue in the develop'ment of that industry, if we are to enter into treaties that will undermine it from year to year? We are only producing 10 per cent of the refined sugar that is necessary to feed our people, and there are many opportunities for the development of this industry in Canada.
I desire to place a few questions on record, and I should like the minister to be good enough to send me answers to these questions before the treaty is proceeded with. My questions are as follows:
1.	What is the duty per pound at present on raw sugar similar in quality to the raw sugar taken from sugar beets coming into Canada from the West Indies and Australia separately, and what will the duty be on said raw sugar when the treaty between Canada and the West Indies now before parliament is consummated?
2.	What was the duty on same grade of raw sugar previous to the reduction of duty on this product in 1923?
3.	How many vessels of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine operate between Canada and the West Indies?
4.	What was the amount lost in operating these vessels each year since they have been placed in that service?
5.	What subsidies, if any, were paid in years 1921, 1922, 1923, 1924, 1926 separately to vessel owners operating between Canada and the West Indies?
6.	Did the minister investigate the effect that this treaty would have on the sugar beet industry before submitting the treaty to parliament?
7.	Why jeopardize the interests of producers in an industry before investigating as to the effect a reduction in tariff would make?
These are some of the questions I should like the minister to answer. I wish to urge upon the minister the need of investigating the extent of the sugar beet industry in our country, the effect that this treaty will have on the producers of sugar beets, and the effect
that these treaties will have on refineries that are located inland, where they will be compelled to carry the raw sugar, if they do carry it at all, long distances in order to compete with those who are able to be served by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.

I pointed out to them that these people did not object so much to the small reduction of sixteen cents per hundred pounds on the raw sugar but that they wanted to bring their sugar in from New York, where they claimed they could get a lower freight rate than if it came in by way of Halifax and St. John, and I had the assurance of the railways that it looked like a reasonable proposition, and that they would see that the refiners out there were not in any worse position than the refiners more favourably located at the ocean or river ports of Canada. The reduction under this agreement on raw sugar which my hon. friend complains of so bitterly is only sixteen cents per hundred pounds on the raw sugar.
What is the total duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is quite true, as my hon. friend said, that the price of beets has dropped, but sugar is just like wheat, oats, butter or cheese, the price is regulated by the world's market, and the price of sugar has

dropped all over the world. I notice that the people of the United States were complaining because their jam industry was suffering on account of the cost of sugar which did not compare with the cost in other markets of the world. That is right, but if my hon. friend happened to come into office he would have to retain that spread of one dollar. I was going to point out in regard to the beet sugar industry that according to the Monthly Bulletin of Agricultural Statistics for September, 1925, this business in Canada has grown considerably. In 1918 there were 18,000 acres under beets in Canada-I am leaving out the odd figures. In 1920 there were 34,000 acres and in 1922 there was a decline to 14,900. In 1924, however, the acreage was back again to 31,000 odd. That shows that the number of acres under cultivation is 
subject to the price obtainable for the product. If a man can obtain more money for wheat or oats or potatoes he will grow those products, and when he can get better prices for beets he will go in for beet growing. It appears, according to this bulletin, that in 1924 two Canadian beet sugar factories were in operation at Chatham and Wallaceburg. A third factory has been established at Raymond, Alberta, by Canadian Sugar Factories, Limited, and the acreage under beets for the past season was 6,634, of which 600 acres were lost and 6,034 thinned. This acreage yielded a total production of 58,000 tons. The business is therefore important.
Complaint has been made that the farmers are compelled to ship their beets to the United States. What is the reason? Let me quote the authority of a gentleman in the employ of the government, of Ontario who spoke recently at a dinner m Winds;! given in honour of the board of trade of that town. He claimed that the local industry was not dealing fairly with the farmers, and he took credit for having induced United States buyers to come over. He stated that the Mount Clemens Sugar Company was contracting for next year at $6 per ton. The company has to pay eighty cents per ton duty, and 'according to this information the farmers will now send their beets to the United States at $6 a ton as compared with $5.50 which the Canadian people were offering. That is why the Canadian beet growers have been shipping their product to the United States: they can get more money for it there. That is also the reason why the cream from my county and others sometimes goes to the United States. The farmer will send his cream or anything else to the market that pays him the most for it.

I was going tc
take up the point the hon. gentleman has just addressed himself to and add slightly to what he has said. The question of the general duty is really the decisive question on the price that the producer of sugar beets gets. As the minister well knows, only a comparatively small fraction of our sugars in the past have come in under specific preferences. That is beyond all room for argument. Sugar being high generally, as my hon. friend has said, and the sugar coming in from the West Indies being only a moiety of the whole, although there was a preference of 82.70 odd per cent given under the contract of 1920, instead of the price per ton of sugar beets going down, as a matter of fadt it went up; but the converse happened in 1923, when with the manufacturers of jams and preserves getting along practically just as well as they are getting along now having regard to the relation of their business to other businesses-I admit their position was not as good as it is now, for we were only then getting over the postwar deflation-and without any real demand for it, the government took half a cent a pound off sugars, and immediately 50 cents a ton was taken off the price of the farmers' beets. That is perfectly obvious because, as I pointed out to my hon. friend the other day when I put my queries to him, the price of the sugar beet to the farmer depends on two things, saccharine content and the price of

raws landed in Canada; and the price of the latter, despite what my hon. friend says, ha3 a great deal to do with tariff arrangements and that sort of thing. It is quite true there is a world price for refined sugar, but this price varies tremendously throughout the world having regard to distributing costs and tariff. It varies very much more having regard to distributing costs than it does in this country in relation to the tariff. And there is a very simple way in which my hon. friend can help our farmers engaged in the sugar beet growing industry practieally'without hurting anybody, because if he studies the tables of refined sugar prices he will not find that the breakfast table gets the benefit of that half cent a pound; it does not. It gets the small benefit here and there which depends far more upon changes in cost of distribution and upon domestic competition than on any change in the price of raws. Therefore if my hon. friend wants to help our farmers who are engaged in the sugar beet growing industry he has just simply to go back to where we were in 1923. If he does that, if he puts up the general rate half a cent, he will find that his treaty here will make but very little difference, if any at all, in that cost.

Let my hon.
friend take his own statistics as to the cost of living in this country, and just see how much our consumers have been benefited by that cut. The lifting of the cost that we have been having recently certainly has not had anything to do with tariff increases; it may have had something to do with tariff reductions, because these are sometimes concurrent with an increased cost of living. In fact we have had that happen. I do not think my hon. friend will find any very close relationship between his tariff on the one hand and his cost of living on the other.
My hon. friend has referred to the American situation. Well, last July there was trouble in the United States about the price of refined sugar. Some of the jam manufacturers thought they were being charged too much for their sugar, and they made application to the President to reduce the sugar duties so as to cut down the price. The President refused the application. In less than six weeks afterwards, notwithstanding that the tariff had been maintained absolutely, the competitive situation of the local market had so developed that there was a substantial

Canada-West Indies Agreement
cut in the domestic price of refined sugar, and the very people who had been urging for a reduction in the tariff ceased their agitation. My hon. friend will find that all reported in the American papers, the conclusion which they drew being that leaving the tariff where it was-and it was high-intensified their local production, as it happened that just as soon as the competitive situation reached a certain point they got their refined sugar at far lower prices than they would have secured if the tariff had been reduced. At any rate, that is what happened there. I repeat, my hon. friend will find a very easy way of helping the people of Lambton and Kent in their sugar beet industry if he will just simply look after what was done in 1923. My hon. friend is more or less engaged in repairing damage done by his government, and he might Quite easily repair this little damage also. By retracing mistaken steps he would not only be improving conditions for his governmental record, but he would be helping things in the country generally.
There was just another point I wanted to refer to. I spoke to my hon. friend the other day in connection with cocoa beans, and I pointed out to him what I believe to be the fact, that with our manufacturers of confectionery and the like, the larger part of their cocoa beans are of a far cheaper quality than the Trinidad cocoa bean. The different parliaments have passed upon this treaty; we are the last to take it up, and I understand from what my hon. friend says that Trinidad is adamant upon this point. The American confectioner is not under the same disability our confectioner is under. Hon. gentlemen here must recollect that we are not now dealing with a preference but with a substantial increase in the duty on cocoa beans coming into Canada. My hon. friend,' with a treaty, is substantially raising the tariff item. Of course if we could get all

A short time ago I think my hon. friend cast some reflection on the service now being operated. For the information of the House I may say that the sendee now under subsidy by the government to what is known as the eastern group of islands has been performed by the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company, who have an office in Halifax. My firm work in conjunction with them. No one realizes more than that company does that the steamers are antiquated and unsuited to the route. That is admitted, and they have felt very deeply the conditions which required them to carry



Canada-West Indies Agreement
on that service with those steamers. It is a reflection on that company, which is one of the largest, most influential and most respected steamship companies in Great Britain. The reason that these ships have been continued on the route is simply that for years past the company has been pressing the government for an improvement in this service. Four or five years ago the government did call for tenders for improved service. That company submitted a tender-the only one submitted-the terms and conditions of which were reasonable, but the government saw fit to turn it down. From time to time, almost from month to month, the government has requested that company to continue the service with the tonnage which has been carrying on that service for twelve or fifteen years past. When the ships were put on they were satisfactory, good enough for the business, for the route and for the passenger traffic. But conditions have changed since then; the ships have grown older and, as I said before, it is a source of annoyance to the company to have to operate them. They were only operated at the urgent request of the government.
In that connection I might say I believe that, as a result of the call by the government for tenders, there will be no offers to perform that entire service. The conditions governing the service to the western group, for which tenders have been asked, are so extreme and so exacting that I am sure no company will undertake it, and no government will pay the subsidy necessary to its operation. But I can quite conceive that with the wonderful picture of the trade that can be done and the expected increase in trade between the western group and this Dominion, the government may be induced to operate ships to carry on that service, and this House and the public will not be aware of the yearly cost the service will entail. It will be extremely expensive. It is held out that there will be a large passenger traffic down there, but I would call attention to the fact that within the last three or four years excusions on the big steamers have become very popular almost throughout the world, and at the present time inducements are being offered by the companies operating on the Atlantic which have arranged for excursions on their large ships from New York and other American ports to the West Indies. In my judgment that will interfere very, very materially with the proposed passenger traffic for the western group. Furthermore, as regards both groups, the tonnage that is now running out to these islands will be increased and [Mr. W. A. Black.J
the number of steamers and the number of trips will be greater than at the present time. The tonnage that is carrying on that trade to-day is running about only sixty per cent full cargo on the average throughout the year. The tonnage now proposed for the western group is eight or ten times greater than the tonnage operating to-day, and how those ships are to be provided with cargo, and where that cargo is to come from, is something that I, and I think those familiar with the West Indies trade, are at a loss to understand. The Royal (Mail, operating on the eastern route, show by their report that their ships have been running on an average sixty-five to sixty-seven per cent short of cargo during the whole year, -and yet it is proposed to increase the carrying capacity on that route under new terms, which can result in nothing else but heavy loss to whoever may be operating the service.
As I said when speaking of this matter before, we are obtaining from the West Indies- I refer now to the eastern group-all the sugar, all the molasses, and all the products of these West India islands that we can consume, and no amount of additional tonnage, not even a daily service can increase our imports from those islands.
So far as outward trade is concerned, the same conditions exist. I do not say there may not be some small increase perhaps in some of the things that are going out there at the present time, but it will not be very great; it will not in any way provide the cargo necessary for the tonnage on that route. This banana trade, of which such a glowing picture has been painted, is in my judgment very problematical. I am perfectly satisfied in my own mind that Canada as a whole cannot be supplied by the proposed services which are to be put on between Jamaica and Canada; I am perfectly satisfied that British Columbia and ithe western portions of this country cannot be supplied. That portion of this country will be supplied, even paying the fifty cents duty, via New Orleans and up the Mississippi valley. The distance and the time taken between Jamaica and New Orleans is about two and one-half days. It is about the same time up the valley, and bananas shipped from Jamaica via New Orleans will reach destination in British Columbia and the western parts of this Dominion before they can reach any Atlantic port, Halifax or St. John. The banana is not only a perishable article, but an article that cannot well be handled in cold weather. The House may know that a banana subjected to a temperature of 55 degrees is blackened and destroyed, and how the trade can be handled to

Canada-West Indies Agreement
advantage in cold weather is something that I cannot understand. The off season in Jamaica has also to be taken into consideration; what are these expensive ships going to carry during that period of four or five months? There is another disadvantage. If there are any fruit dealers here, they will know perfectly well that the Jamaica banana is inferior in quality to that of British Honduras.

Inferior to those of almost
every island to the south.

Yes, and not only that: in Jamaica they have their dry seasons when the banana crop is not worth transporting. What are the ships to do for cargo under those circumstances? There is another point: We all know that Jamaica suffers from hurricanes, A few years ago we all read of the island being swept by hurricanes and the banana crop being blown down. Where is the fruit to come from then? This proposal in connection with Jamaica is but the dream of an idealist, which will never materialise, and it will cost this country millions of dollars.
I would also refer to an antiquated proposal in connection with this treaty, a proposal that has been tried in the West, Indies and condemned and abandoned. In the early days before there was much competition among the steamship lines, the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company operated under subsidy from the imperial government from Southampton to Barbados. When these boats from Southampton arrived at Barbados, their cargo was transferred to what were called the interinsular boats, which distributed the cargo among the islands, one going to the islands north, one to Grenada, and one down to Demerara. What happened? As competition increased, other linrs came into the West Indies trade; they carried their cargoes direct to these islands that were being served by the inter-insular boats, and the result was that no shipper would put his goods on a boat when they had to be transferred to another boat. He could ship on a steamer going direct to destination, and the result was that these inter-insular boats were left without cargo and were withdrawn.
It is proposed under the treaty to have a service under which cargo from Canada will be transferred to another steamship at Jamaica, whence it will proceed to British Honduras. If that is done it will be necessary to provide warehouses and all sorts of docking facilities at Kingston, Jamaica, as well as officials to look after the boat. Mr. Chairman, I think it would be wise on the part of the committee to pass this item. I understand that the parties interested in the proposition are still working on it, and hope eventually to be able to establish a plant in Manitoba for the manufacture of twine and other products. I should like to see the item pass because I think it will help to encourage an industry which we have been seeking to establish in Manitoba for quite a number of years.

Mr. Chairman, the difficulty is not in connection with the growth of hemp. When I say that I am relying on the word of the government, because the government were in charge of what was going on and were checking off the tests that were made. I am relying, as I recollect, on the word of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), that good hemp could be grown in Manitoba, that in fact he had seen magnificent hemp growing there. I think we had similar testimony from the other minister from the west (Mr. Stewart). Apparently there was no question but what this country could produce excellent hemp, and that there was ample room for a plant to manufacture hemp into twine and other products, the only difficulty being in starting such a plant. That was common ground. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture nods his head; his memory and mine are exactly the same with respect to the matter. The difficulty was that while Colonel Grassie with his associates from Manitoba were perfectly firm as to the minimum assistance which would be required, the department

Supply-Trade and Commerce
thought that that assistance could be pared. The difficulty, as I recollect, took on two phases; one was as to the amount per annum, and the other as to the number of years and the manner in which the bounty would taper. As a matter of fact, the difference between the department and the expert which these gentlemen brought out from Ireland was very, very small; but I know the Irish expert when he left the country said that the government had effectually killed the scheme which they were ostensibly trying to help; that by withholding but very little they were effectually ensuring that Manitoba would not get this industry.
In connection with this item, Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that the government make it workable. The government has on its files now the representations made, and they have had two and a half years of failure. They have information that this is an industry which ought to be developed; they have acted upon that information and are committed to that position. Why should not my hon. friend make his act workable this year? It would be an easy thing to do and as I recall it, the amount involved is practically trifling. If the government really have faith in this venture, after playing with it for two and a half years, why not make sure that something will be done to give this new industry to a province which should have it?
