speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was just going to make an explanation. I understand that under the act we have to take a census every five years in the three western provinces, and the additional amount this year is to provide for that extra expenditure. This vote provides for:
General contingencies of the bureau, including salaries of temporary employees, criminal and vital statistics, travelling expenses of the Dominion statistician and his staff; freight and express; telephone and telegraph ; newspapers and periodicals; rental of
tabulating and sorting machines	
Completion of 1921 census (6th Census).. ..
1926 Census
Field work (actual cost of 1921 census of prairie provinces, plus 15 per cent).. ..
We have added fifteen per cent to the cost of the 1921 census of the prairie provinces, and the amount is $415,000. There is also the temporary staff at Ottawa, $80,000, and contingencies and stationery, $10,000.

I understand that this
census is taken in the three prairie provinces under an act, passed some years ago, and it has the effect of automatically increasing the annual subsidies to these provinces every five years, instead of every ten years, as is the case in other provinces. Why should that position obtain? It is an unfair advantage that the three prairie provinces have over the other provinces. The other provinces have to wait until the decennial census is taken before they get any increase. Of course it may be urged that this is a part of a bargain, but I do not see how it can be a bargain, because they were not provinces, as I recollect it, at the time this legislation was passed.
Is it the intention of the government to follow the practice adopted in 1921 by the late government when census enumerators were appointed and to see that those enumerators are selected, wherever possible, other things being equal, from returned soldiers? That practice was adopted in New Brunswick with very marked success, and the men who did the work did it as well as it was ever done- perhaps better. I commend the suggestion to my hon. friend-it is in his department-that the enumerators for the census be not employed simply because they are supporters of a certain party, but that returned soldiers be appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the commissioner will probably follow the same procedure as was adopted in 1921.

But will he be
allowed to do it?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend I have not time to interfere with him.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
But there are others.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In answer to the question of my hon. friend (Mr. Hanson) as to why the census is taken every five years instead of every ten years, it is because in 1918 an act was put through providing for it.
But previous to that time was there any such legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There has been a decennial census for some time. I imagine Sir George Foster brought it in because of demands made from western Canada, and it is quite a reasonable proposition. The drift of immigration coming into the country has been going largely to the western provinces. They have on that account to provide additional schools and highways and additional expenses are involved in that country.

If we take to heart what we have heard from our friends on my left for the last three or four years-not this year, but previously-we would imagine that the country was going to the bow-wows. I listened to the lamentation of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) when he sat in the centre of the House, that the western country was going behind. Has there been a natural increase in the population of western Canada since this government came into power, or is it on a par with the other provinces in that respect? I see no reason why the prairie provinces should have the census taken every five years, any more than the other provinces should. If they have it, we should have it. I do not see why any province should have it. It is an additional expense the country should dispense with, and the proper course is to repeal the act and save half a million dollars.
May I ask whether all the census enumerators have not already been appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I really do not know, but I imagine they have been, because they have to get dawn to work very soon.
I understand every one of them has been appointed.
Are they appointed by the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I think not.
On whose recommendation? Are they appointed by order in council?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think so.
Are they appointed by the local member, or does the defeated1 candidate send in his recommendation to the patronage committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know that there is
such a thing as a patronage committee. I understand the commissioner has followed the same course as he did in 1921.

I understand the minister
made the appointments.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, I have not found any
order in council.

That is the information I
have.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Has the hon. member a nomination to make?
I had one or two applications to make, and I was instructed every position was filled.

I made a suggestion to
the minister which he ought to consider seriously, and! that is the repeal of the act providing for the census in the prairie provinces every five years. He will save the taxpayers of the country at least half a million dollars every five years, and that will go down as an eternal monument to him. The matter is worthy of consideration, if he can save the treasury that much money every year.

The population
of western Canada has not been going down; it has been increasing continuously. This census will show a big increase. I think the act should remain as it is, and that we should have opr five-year census. The longer this government stays in power the more immigration will come into the country.

I do not think I said that the population of the three prairie provinces had been going down, but I quoted the representatives from the prairie provinces in the last three years who stated that such was the case.
The hon. gentleman spoke of lamentations. The only lamentations we have heard have been from the party sitting to the left of the Speaker.
DRAYTON: The hon. member, who has been here such a short time, does not know anything about the history of his province.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
He was bom in it.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

Here is another gentleman who does not know anything about what is 'being said here. He only knows the Progressives on the public platform when he calls them names. But I really rose to ask whether the answer of the minister is really serious when he refers to the legislation of 1918 as the legislation which made necessary this expenditure. I am inclined to think that the legislation of 1918 was merely legislation which had to do with the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, and which simply continued an existing statutory requirement. It is entirely wrong to proceed on the idea that this is a new thing.
It is part of the legislation of 1905.
I am inclined to think so.

May I ask
when these enumerators begin their work?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The act respecting the Dominion Bureau of Statistics provides that a census of population and agriculture in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta shall be taken by the bureau under the direction of the minister, on a date in the month of June in the year 1926, to be fixed by the Governor in Council, and every tenth year thereafter.
They begin their work in June. Can the minister tell me how many officials or enumerators are required for this work, and how many have already been appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The following is a report of the Civil Service Commission on the subject:
The Civil Service Commission has under consideration the question of the selection of the necessary staff for the taking of the quinquennial census for the prairie provinces, 1926. These appointments are of a temporary nature and consist of two divisions: (1) The census commissioners and census enumerators located dn the prairie provinces; approximately 2,400 census enumerators will be required, whose term of employment will not usually exceed thirty days. There will also be about fifty-five census commissioners, one for each census district, who will be employed for a period not exceeding six months. The census commissioners and enumerators for the Dominion census of 1921 were exempted under section 38a from the provisions of the Civil Service Act, P.C. 2526, October 23, 1920, and the selection of these employees was left to the Department of Trade and Commerce, P.C. 1205, April 12, 1921.
It is recommended that a similar procedure be followed in the case of the quinquennial census for the prairie provinces 1926, and that the temporary census commissioners and enumerators be exempted from the operation of the Civil Service Act, and the selection of these employees be made by the Department of Trade and Commerce.
On this occasion the procedure of 1921 is being followed.
Have any of these officials been appointed yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I fancy they have.
How many?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hope they have all been appointed, because they must get to work and it is necessary that they be instructed first.
They do not get to work until June.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, but they must be schooled in April. My hon. friend knows that in every census a man must be sent from the department to instruct the commissioners in the rules, and these commissioners must meet the various enumerators.

If they have been appointed already for the purpose of this schooling to which the minister refers, that brings up another point. On whose recommendation have they been appointed, and do these recommendations come from the various localities? I might ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Dunning) who sits immediately behind the Minister of Finance to inform the committee, if he can, whether any of these officials were appointed in Regina a short time ago, and if so, how many?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Probably my hon. friend was not following me while I was reading the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission that the procedure of 1921 be followed.
If the appointments are made by the minister's department, who in that department makes them?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Coats makes them on the recommendations he receives, and naturally he will consult with the people in that part of the country.

I understand from Mr. Coats that he does not make the appointments. I gathered from what the minister read and from what he stated, that his own department makes them, and not the Bureau of Statistics, although I may be wrong in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When the matter was brought to my attention I asked an officer in my department to consult with the representatives of western Canada and have the nominations made so as to get the matter concluded. I have not heard from him since.
That does not meet my point.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend was here in 1921 when the nominations were made at that time.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

My point is that if the nominations rest with the department, whether the department obtains recomendations from the Bureau of Statistics or not, the appointments have been made by the department. I want to know who actually made those appointments or who has knowledge of their making.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend has recommendations to make and the positions are not all filled, I shall be glad to consider suggestions.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: One practical suggestion was made by an hon. member opposite with reference to the vote before the House, namely, that the amount might be reduced by means of an amendment to the act wh\h provides for a quinquennial census in th* prairie provinces, in place of the decennial census which is taken throughout the rest of Canada. I have looked into the matter and I find that the quinquennial census in the prairie provinces is provided for in the acts creating those provinces. Constitutional lawyers in the House will correct me if I am wrong, but in my opinion this House cannot now amend those acts. An imperial act is necessary to amend the autonomy legislation creating the western provinces inasmuch as they are now under the provisions of the British North America Act.
They did not hesitate when the autonomy acts were passed to override the spirit and letter of the British North America Act.

What purpose does the expenditure of this $500,000 really accomplish? What service is rendered by the taking of the census? The three prairie provinces get an annual subsidy from the Dominion of some five or six hundred dollars. Would it not be better to vote that money to the provinces direct instead of spending it in an idle manner, such as is proposed, for patronage purposes? Give us the $500,000 direct. It would be of greater benefit to the provinces than it can be when spent in the way suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) has pointed out, this matter is subject to the British North America Act, and any amendment can be made only by an imperial statute. My hon. friend (Mr. Rogers) asks me what service is accomplished. Well, the Department of Finance will know that next year when an additional claim is put in.
(Mr. Robb.]
But you can save an added subsidy by dividing the $500,000 among the provinces now.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. member suggest an amendment to the act?

The Minister of Railways has said that we have an act of parliament which is subject to amendment only by imperial legislation, in respect of the quinquennial census. What disturbs my mind is this question:	What purpose is served by
taking a five-year census rather than a census every ten years? Does it mean that if the population increases in the western provinces we shall increase the subsidy accordingly?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is so.

If the result of taking that census does not involve some such readjustment, why do we take it? If it is merely a duplication of work, I say the expenditure is excessive and unnecessary. If, on the other hand, the statute which we have validated in this House requires amendment, and can only be amended by act of the imperial parliament, I submit we should take appropriate steps to that end. Is not that reasonable? For what purpose are we voting this money? I care not whether the census enumerators entertain political opinions favourable to that side or to this side of the House; that does not appeal to me in any way; what I am thinking of is the unnecessary expenditure of public money. If we can prevent we should do so.

Mr. Chairman,
last night I heard the hon. member for Argen-teuil (Sir George Perley) announce that we could get the British North America Act amended at any time we desired. Here is an opportunity to ask the imperial parliament to take action. Then we could save the money covered by this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I had no other intention than to state what were the facts with regard to the possibility of this parliament repealing the provisions affecting the quinquennial census in the prairie provinces. As to what the quinquennial census accomplishes with respect to those provinces, I read from the Saskatchewan act, section 18, subsection B:
A census of the said proivnce shall be taken in every fifth year reckoning from the general census of 1901, and an approximate estimate of the population shall be made at equal intervals of time between each quinquennial and decennial census; and whenever the population, by any such census or estimate, exceeds 250,000, which shall be the minimum upon which the said allowance shall be calculated, the amount of the said allowance shall be increased accordingly, and so on, until the population has reached 800,000 souls.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Then of course the terms of the general act apply. Now, as to the effect of the coming census, may I say with respect to the province with which I am most familiar that at the census of 1921, if I recollect correctly, the population of Saskatchewan was 757,810. On the basis mentioned in the section which I have read, which provides for an estimate to be made by the Bureau of Statistics at equal periods between the quinquennial and decennial census, we are now being paid a subsidy on a population of 828,600, so that an increase in population in two and a half years from 757,000 to .828,000 has been recognized by the authorities who have to do with this matter. I am satisfied from mv knowledge of conditions in the west, and I feel sure that other members on both sides of the House will bear me out, that the 1926 census will demonstrate a further steady growth in proportion to the growth to which I have just been referring. As far as the item itself is concerned, we cannot change it; we are bound by statute to provide for it. As to appealing to the imperial parliament, I feel sure they would want to know what the provinces concerned thought about amending the conditions under which they entered confederation.

I am not
quite clear why the minister brings in the imperial parliament. The bills of 1905 were passed by this parliament and as far as I know they have never been ratified by the imperial parliament. They are therefore in every sense Canadian statutes, if I understand correctly.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I must leave that to the decision of the constitutional lawyers in the House.

Did the minister quote
from an imperial or federal act?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: An act of this parliament.

Mr. Chairman, if the taking of the census is to establish the rate at which Saskatchewan is to be paid, it is not treating the province fairly not to take the census, so I do not think we need bother about the law. If the payment of the subsidy to Saskatchewan depends upon that, I think we should certainly let the item pass.
Hear, hear.
I wish my good friends opposite had deferred their applause just for a moment. I was going to suggest that probably the province of Saskatchewan will be in no danger since the appointments are made.

May I ask the Minister of
Railways if he will show as much concern for the province of Nova Scotia with regard to the terms under which it came into confederation?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, so far as I can I shall be happy to give consideration to the fairness of any matter presented to this House by any hon. member on behalf of any province.
I am glad to know it.

May I pursue that thought of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Quinn) a little further and ask the Minister of Railways if he will extend similar consideration to the reduction of freight rates, a subject that he dilated upon in Winnipeg the other day?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is out of order.

There is no doubt at all that we have to take the census, although it is not for the reason given by the hon. Minister of Railways. He need not raise any bogey about imperial acts or anything of the kind. AVe take the census because it is provided for by our own law. But notwithstanding that fact, with great deference to the minister I submit that the item can be discussed. For example, we might discuss why it is that the amount is increased $85,000 over the grant made in 1921. What is the reason for the increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The estimate was made up by the census commissioner who has been taking the census for a number of years. He added 15 per cent to the previous estimate.
But what is the basis of the 15 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I assume he estimates it on the growth of the population. He does not necessarily spend the money.
What is the rate of remuneration paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The rates and classification are the same as in 1921: Census clerks: grade 1, $780; grade 2, $840; grade 3, $900. Census audit clerks: grade 1, $960; grade 2, $1,020; grade 3, $1,080. As in the Dominion census of 1921, it is intended that eligibles shall be appointed as census clerks grade 1 and census audit clerks grade 1, and be promoted to the higher grades as their services warrant.
But that has to do with the office clerks here, as I followed my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Possibly.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
If he will just remember what his learned colleague the Minister of Railways was telling him, what is he going to pay the commissioners in the first place, and then the enumerators?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
While the minister is
looking that up, might I just read the authority for the bogey which my hon. friend-

I thought we
were rid of that. If you like, we can argue it; if the hon. member wants to kill time he can do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This is a matter of some importance. I am not one of the learned members of the House, as is my hon. friend, but I can at least read the English language.
Hurrah.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I read now from section 6 of the British North America Act, 1871, an amendment to the act which is entitled "An Act Respecting the Establishment of Provinces in the Dominion of Canada" and which empowers and sets forth the terms under which this parliament may create new provinces in Canada. Section 6 reads as follows:
Except as provided by the third section, of this act, it shall not be competent for the parliament of Canada to alter the provisions of the last-mentioned act of the said parliament in so far as it relates to the province of Manitoba, or of any other act hereafter establishing new provinces in the said Dominion, subject always to the right of the legislature of the province of Manitoba to alter from time to time the provisions of any law respecting the qualification of electors and members of the legislative assembly, and to make laws respecting elections in the said province.
As I say, I am not a constitutional lawyer, but surely the language is plain:
It shall not be competent for the parliament of Canada to alter the provisions of the last-mentioned act of the said parliament in so far as it relates to the province of Manitoba, or of any other act hereafter establishing new provinces in the said Dominion.
I am not arguing, Mr. Chairman; I am merely stating what is taken to be a fact.
As I said before, there is no necessity for raising the bogey. It is our act and we observe it.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This is the British North America Act, an imperial act of 1871.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend does not argue this point seriously, does he?
I do not know what my hon. friend is talking about. I am not arguing anything.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend is not arguing Why does he not sit down?
My hon. friend-

Mr. Chairman, I can
quite understand the reason for a quinquennial census being taken some years ago. At that time the new provinces were adding to their population rapidly, and perhaps it was an uncertain stage. It seems to me that at that time it was fair to have a quinquennial census, but now conditions are more stabilized; we have not the same rapid growth in those provinces and the occasion for such a frequent census does not now exist. Of course it is the law, but if it is to the advantage of everyone to do so, the law may be changed. I understand that the subsidy per capita increase from the Dominion government for five years amounts to less than $500,000. Perhaps the Minister of Railways would inform me of the difference in those amounts.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: May I be permitted?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: If the cost for the three prairie provinces is as estimated, $500,000 for the quinquennial census, the increase in each of the three prairie provinces multiplied by 80 cents per head for each of the years involved would be the aggregate sum for comparison. I cannot tell my hon. friend what that would be, but offhand one would say it would amount to more than $500,000 in the course of five years.

I cannot say what the
amount is, only I have been informed that the actual increase would not exceed, $500,000. That may not be, but there is not much difference between the two figures, and therefore I suggest that it is very poor business to expend $500,000 for the purpose of granting the three prairie provinces another $500,000 or thereabouts. And I think it is well worth the attention of the minister to consider whether some change, which would not interfere with the grants given to the three prairie provinces, might not save a considerable sum of money.

Just a word in regard to the quinquennial census. There were two objects in view when the legislation of 1905 was passed. The quinquennial census was enacted in that year in the first place for the purpose of fixing the representation of the new provinces. It was provided by section 6 of the act that the representation of Alberta and of Saskatchewan should be fixed at the next quinquennial census, which would be in the year 1911, and the proportion of representation was fixed by section 6. But it was only for that

Supply-Trade and Commerce
particular year, 1911, because subsection 2 oi section 6 says:
The representation of the said province shall thereafter be readjusted from time to time according to the provisions of section 51 of the British North America Act, 1867.
So that the quinquennial census, since 1911, has had nothing to do with the representation of the new provinces. That is now adjusted in accordance with section 51 of the British North America Act, which provides for adjustment after every decennial census. The other purpose of the quinquennial census was in regard to the fixing of the subsidy, but the period has arrived when that is of no effect in regard to Saskatchewan. It is provided that when Saskatchewan has a population of 800,000 there shall be no progressive readjustment of the subsidy. The last clause of section 18 .
1 U V 1UOO .
The amount of the said allowance shall be increased accordingly.
That is, from $250,000 up.
-and so on until the population has reached 800,000 souls.
There is an exactly similar provision in the Alberta act. If Saskatchewan had a population of less than 800,000, we could do nothing but take the quinquennial census, but I understand it is admitted by the Bureau of Statistics and by the government itself that there were, two and a half years ago, 829,000 souls in the province of Saskatchewan. Consequently their subsidy is fixed, as is the subsidy of every other province of Canada, so there is no necessity for a census in that province at present. In Alberta the case is different: the population of Alberta has not reached the 800,000 mark, therefore we are bound to take the census for the purpose of fixing the subsidy, but not for the purpose of representation in this House. I think the minister would be well advised to reconsider this measure and provide that no census be taken in Saskatchewan, if it be so that the population has already been ascertained as over the 800,000 mark.

The Minister of Railways has created a rather impossible barrier by the contention that any act altering the provision for the quinquennial census would have to be an imperial act. He admitted that he was not a constitutional lawyer. If he will read section 146 of the British North America Act dealing with the creation of other provinces, and then turn to the very act from which he has read, which is the British North America Act of 1871, he will see in section 2 that:
The parliament of Canada may from time to time eatablish new provinces in any territories forming for
the time being (part of tihe Dominion of Canada, but not included in any province thereof, and may, at the time of such establishment, make provision for the constitution and administration of any such province, and for the passing of laws for the peace, order, and good government of such province, and for its representation in the said parliament.
So the inherent jurisdiction rests with the parliament of Canada to make a law dealing with just such a question as that to which the minister has referred, and I submit that, apart from the contention of the last speaker with respect to the abandonment of the vote, consideration should be given to the wisdom of extending the time for taking the census and making it co-ordinate with the census taken in the other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Dealing with the point made by my hon. friend from South Wellington, that the province of Saskatchewan does not now neea a quinquennial census because it has passed the 800,000 population mark, which is given in the Saskatchewan laet and in the Alberta act as the limit for change under their per capita subsidy, I would again call his attention to section 20 of the same act, which provides for compensation in lieu of the lands of these provinces which were retained by the Dominion at the time the provinces were created. There he will find:
Inasmuch as the said province will not have the public land as a source of revenue, there shall be paid iby Canada to the province by half-yearly payments, in advance, an annual sum based upon the population of the province as from time to time ascertained by the quinquennial census thereof, as follows
The population of the said province being assumed to be at present two hundred and fifty thousand.
And so on. It provides that thereafter, until such population reaches 800,000, the sum payable shall be such and such; and thereafter, until such population reaches 1,200,000 the sum payable shall be such and such. It is important therefore to continue the engagement with the province of Saskatchewan. - In quoting this in the first place I was not speaking from the point of view of the province of Saskatchewan, but merely with a desire that the House should be clear with respect to something with which I happened to be familiar. So far as the other two provinces are concerned, they have not even yet reached the 800.000 population mark, which is important to them with respect to the per capita subsidy. We must consider them also.
In regard to the point raised by my hon. friend from Vancouver South, the act from which I read, the British North America Act, 1871, was an amending act, amending the act from which my hon. friend read.

No, I read from the amending act of 1871.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

As I said before, I really think there is no necessity for anything except making speeches on this question. There is our act, and we have to live up to it, and we intend to; there is no question about that, and all this to the contrary is just so much of a bogey. The duty is upon this parliament, as I see it, to carry out this quinquennial census. If the Solicitor General had been in when I was speaking before, he would have known that I was not making an argument; I was simply saying we were bound to do it, but with his customary lightheartedness he rushed in and said something that was wrong. He is not often wrong, but we all make mistakes sometimes. But let us get down to the business of this item. I was asking the minister what the rate of remuneration was to the different gentlemen who are going to get employment. We have not yet found out how they are employed, what qualifications are required, who is recommending them, or anything else.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The rates are to be exactly the same as in 1921. I will give my hon. friend a memorandum of the expenditure in 1921. There were 243 commissioners; their allowance was $77,500; travelling expenses and disbursements, $13,009.96; recording, $113,451.80, or a total of $203,961.76. Then for field work for the general census-
That is more extended.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will get that for my hon.
friend if he desires.

My hon. friend seems to have given a very excellent reason why he can assist himself as Minister of Finance. The whole cost of doing this work in the 1921 general census, when more particulars have to be taken, was only $415,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh no.
I took that figure down, that the cost of the census work in the three prairie provinces in 1921 was $415,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. The 1921 census was the general census, and the cost of the field work was $1,184,652.10.
That is for the whole country?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The cost of the general census of 1921 was $2,122,052.

Can my hon.
friend tell me where he gets that item of $415,000 as the cost for 1921?
'[DOT]Mr. Ladner.]

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That was the estimate they
gave me for this work. The actual cost of the 1921 census in the prairie provinces was $415,000. Then there is the temporary staff at Ottawa, $80,000; contingencies, stationery, punch cards, telegrams and so forth, $10,000. This estimate of the cost of the field work anticipates approval of the rates that prevailed in 1921.
Is this correct, that $415,000 is not an exact figure at all, but merely an estimate?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Merely an estimate.
Then I do not press it. My hon. friend has not told me, for example, how many of these gentlemen who have been appointed are returned soldiers.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not give that information.
That was the rule that was observed before, and we were to have the same rule obtaining this time. I think we should know whether the rule is being followed.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would say offhand, although I do not know, that any man in western Canada who did not follow that rule might find himself in trouble with the people in western Canada, because there is no part of Canada that contributed so largely to our effort overseas as the western prairie provinces.

Do I understand the minister to say that the cost of the last decennial census in all Canada was something over $1,000,000, and that the cost in the three prairie provinces was something over $400,000? Surely that cannot be right. The cost of taking the census in the three prairie provinces could not amount to nearly half the cost of taking the census all over Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have this estimate given me by the statistician who conducts the census. The total expenditure for the census of 1911 was $1,316,415.35. The expenditure for the 1921 census was $2,122,052.

Is that for the field work
or was it the total expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They did not give me that
information.

I understood the minister to say the cost of the field work for the Dominion was something over a million dollars, and that of the field work for the three prairie provinces $415,000. It seems

Supply-Trade and Commerce
incomprehensible to us that the cost of the field work for the three prairie provinces should1 be approximately 40 per cent of the whole. There must be some mistake about that, or else the rate of wages there is higher.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, there is no higher rate of pay. The work is paid for at so much per head, and I have heard repeated complaints from the field met. that they do not get enough for the services they perform. It is not a question of paying so much per month, it is a question of the work performed and the names turned in.

Has there been any increase in the amount asked for in connection with the Bureau of Statistics? While I am on my feet I should like to say that while I do not avail myself very much of the activities of the bureau-and I rather think I should because I believe it is a very excellent institution-I have heard in days gone by numerous complaints from merchants, manufacturers and employers of labour that the multiplicity of the demands made by the bureau for statistics has proven to be a perfect nuisance to the office managers of those concerns. The concerns in question are threatened with dire pains and penalties if they do not fill up the forms forwarded to them and give the information asked for. Now, it is necessary for every country to have some system of statistics and these statistics are sometimes of very great value. But the difficulty probably in this case is that the Bureau of Statistics is embracing too many subjects, requiring too much information, and taking up too murih of the available time of commercial executives. I have in my mind one of the largest pulp and paper concerns of the country whose secretary is not only assistant general manager, but discharges a multitude of other duties. This gentleman tells me that the demands made upon him from time to time by the Bureau of Statistics are overwhelming. I wish the minister would give some attention to the complaint. Perhaps the existing system could be simplified. The complaint is not a new one; I know that in days gone by it has been voiced by other members on both sides of the House. Perhaps the minister would look into the matter and see if he cannot devise some method which will remove these complaints on the part of businessmen.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will.

Has the government under consideration negotiations with the province of Saskatchewan similar to those conducted with 14011-117J	*
Alberta as to the question of natural resources? May I ask also whether the subsidy will be paid to Alberta when it receives back its natural resources?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The latter question might
very properly be answered. My hon. friend's first question has nothing whatever to do with this matter, although if I had the information I would willingly give it to him. I think the arrangement made with Alberta was tabled and is available to my hon. friend.

Cannot my hon. friend yet tell me how the men for this work are appointed, how many there are, and on whose recommendation they are chosen? We are voting this money; we have got to spend it, and we might just as well find out how it is to be disbursed-and how these appointments are to be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have already stated-perhaps my hon. friend was out at the time-that when the commissioner asked for recommendations I instructed my secretary to see the western men, and I have not heard from him since. I imagine the appointments have been made on the recommendations of western men. At any rate, I hope they have all been made because I do not want to be bothered with them any more. Let me say this to my hon. friend in all seriousness:	If the conditions
were reversed and my hon. friend were over here I would not challenge his judgment as to making the appointments.
I am not going to challenge my hon. friend's judgment at all. The trouble is that he has never exercised it.
Order.

I wonder if it is an offence to take a minister of this government, whose veracity I happen to believe in, at his word? It is not so many moments since the hon. gentleman said that when applications came in for appointments all he did with them was to hand them to his officials and ask them to get the views of western members thereon, that he did not want to be bothered with them. Because I take the hon. gentleman at his word his supporters are so amazed that they call "order".

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: You need not get mad, though.

There really is at least one minister of this government whose word the House can accept, but apparently
184$

Supply-Trade and Commerce
his supporters are amazed at the fact. Now my hon. friend said he has not appointed these people; he has deferred the matter to his officials; he has given gentlemen from the west-and I do not know what gentlemen- the right of making these appointments. I do not think my hon. friend has got the list, I do not believe he knows anything about it. I am of the opinion that instead of the minister taking the responsibility of making these appointments the matter has been handed over to "the best political organization in the west" and if our reports are true "the best political organization in the west" is now represented here. Perhaps we should ask that political organization for the list; the minister has not got it. Surely the committee is entitled to a little better information than that. If my hon. friend has not made these appointments-and he says he has not-we are entitled to know who has made them. Surely the House is entitled to know a little bit about the country's business, what the qualification for these appointments were, and whether or not the returned soldier is being looked after in connection with them? My hon. friend does not know. Perhaps some of these gentlemen from the west can tell us whom they appointed.

I have no wish to hold up this vote, but in view of the practice established in 1921 when returned men were given the preference, and the statement that the department has the appointing of these men, I should like to know if the minister can state now or at some future time what percentage of the appointees are returned men.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall be glad to do that
I will bring down also a complete return, if it is available, with respect to the appointments of 1921. I do not admit they are all returned soldiers, but I accept my hon. friend's word.

Nobody said they were
all returned soldiers. What was said was that, other things being equal, where returned men were available they were appointed. In my constituency that rule was carried out to the letter.
Mr. STEWART (Edmonton) Surely my hon. friend had nothing to do with the appointments in 1921.

I happened to have the
misfortune of running an election just before the census was taken, and had to run another one just after it was taken.

I rise to make a correction. The Minister of Railways pointed out to me that the act of 1905 in respect to Alberta and Saskatchewan, which he and I were discussing, had actually been superseded in regard to the question of provincial subsidies iby the act in amendment of the British North America Act in 1907, on an address of the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada. By the British North America Act, 1907, these subsidies are now fixed in all provinces according to population, starting with a population of 150,000, and running up to a population of 1,500,000, but with respect to Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, the quinquennial census i3 still the determining factor as to population. I see now the necessity of taking the quinquennial census, as the British North America Act, 1907, is based on the population, and the population for the three prairie provinces has to be fixed by the quinquennial census.

I do not know whether my hon. friend has yet given me the information I asked for. Can 'he not give me a list of the names? Can he not give at least the names of the commissioners who have to carry on this business? Surely there is not such a mystery about how it is being done that the information is kept secret from the minister. I am not asking for a list of a host of small employees, but I do submit that it is the easiest thing in the world to say who the commissioners are and who is responsible; for their employment. It is ridiculous thlat we should be asked to pass this item, providing, as it does, for the appointment of a whole lot of commissioners who are already appointed, not by the minister, but on the say-so of certain western gentlemen, and to pass it without the granting of a reasonable request for information.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will undertake to give my
hon. friend a complete list of the commissioners. He does not want the enumerators.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And if he desires it, I shall
be glad to table the list of 1921. I will take the responsibility for the nominations in my department and say frankly, "upon the recommendation of so and so."

With regard to the
point raised by the hon. member (Mr. Hanson), I think we al appreciate the very excellent work the statistical branch performs, but I would urge that some consideration be given to those from whom a large variety

Supply-Trade and Commerce
of statistics are received. Anyone who has had anything to do with business organizations-and I think the Minister of Finance will agree with me in this-will realize that for ten or twelve years there has been a burden imposed on office organizations that has increased the clerical cost of carrying on the ordinary business of the country by forty to fifty per cent, due to the amount of statistics continually being asked for. In order to comply with these requests it is almost impossible for an ordinary business man to do anything else than furnish statistical records, many of which are never looked at after they are compiled, because they are of no public, service whatever. They do not accomplish anything; there is a considerable cost for compiling, printing and so on, and in reality they serve no real purpose.

The impression I had from the minister's statement was that he would give the western members a chance of submitting some names, and I was going to ask him if he would delay bringing down the list until I have had a chance of submitting names.

I find myself very much out of harmony with my hon. friend in his criticism of the Bureau of Statistics. I think it is one of the best departments of the government and that it should be maintained. Speaking for the group in this section of the House, we make use of these statistics to a great extent, and I think it is very important that we should have those figures available, compiled regularly as they are, at stated intervals. They are reliable and accurate, and I would protest strongly against any effort to reduce the efficiency of that bureau. I ask the minister if there is any reduction in the estimates for the bureau itself this year. The amount for the Bureau of Statistics and the amount for the census are under the one head, and it is rather difficult to know whether there has been any reduction in the amount for the bureau itself.

I appreciate the work of the Bureau of Statistics as thoroughly as my hon. friend or any other hon. member. I do not want to see the Bureau of Statistics made less efficient, but I am confident that it can in reality be made more efficient in matters of vital concern, leaving out matters of detailed statistics which can be of no public service whatever. There is not a business office in this country that is not called upon to furnish periodically all through the year a mass of details which cannot serve any public purpose. If only the essentials are
looked after, the Bureau of Statistics will be able to give my hon. friend and his friends all the information they require on matters of a public character; it will render a service to this House and to the country and will place no unnecessary burden on business organizations and executives. The statistics we got ten years ago were just as satisfactory as those which are furnished to us now; but if you go into any industrial concern in this country you will find that their office overhead has been increased forty or fifty per cent by the necessity for making this detailed information available. The gathering of detailed statistics has become a municipal, provincial and federal hobby, and I expect that when I go home I shall find a form waiting to be filled out giving the colour of my employees' hair, the shade of their eyes, and every other personal detail, however trifling. That limit will soon be reached.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For once I find myself on a question of public importance exactly in accord with my hon. friend. I have on more than one occasion taken this matter up with the Dominion Statistician and he has replied that, while no doubt it might be annoying to some individual employer to be asked to engage a few extra clerks to provide the information, it was nevertheless a fact that the information was required.

There is some merit in what the minister has to say, and those who are in business have not much fault to find with the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. But I want to say to my hon. friend (Mr. Campbell), in confirmation of the remarks of the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson), that there is too much duplication of requests of a like nature from different branches of the bureau with regard to the operations of various industries throughout the Dominion. All hon. members are no doubt acquainted with the census of industry', the information contained in which is compiled by the bureau from information derived from industries and business institutions. After a firm has given the necessary information for this compilation, along comes the Chemical and Metallurgical branch of the bureau with a demand of the same people, who happen to be engaged in some other industry, for precisely the same information with regard to capital, plant, repairs, maintenance, raw material consumed, the amount of labour involved, the quantity of fuel and supplies of all kinds used, and so forth. All that information has already been supplied to the census of industry, and within a week it has to be given to the Chemical and
1S50

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Metallurgical branch of the bureau. The dates are not always the same, nor are the items of information in exactly the same categorical order, but the industry is put to a good deal of trouble in getting the facts and figures called for.
The hon. member (Mr. Nicholson) is on perfectly safe ground. In my opinion the time has come for a co-ordination of all efforts of the various departments of the Bureau of Statistics, in order to obviate all the trouble to which industry and business concerns are put in supplying information. We are obliged to supply the reports asked for; if they are not provided, a penalty ensues. The same information which is given to the Bureau of Statistics is given, we find, to the Department of Labour.
Let us abolish that.

That might not be a bad idea. I may inform the minister that businessmen generally have expressed the view on many occasions that there should be some consolidation of these statistics. I know of one industry which has been obliged to forward three times over to the federal government, in the course of one year, the same information in different forms. For example, the Department of Labour asks for a weekly return showing the number of employees, male and female, together with a statement as to the hours they work, and when you come to the census of industry you find detailed information demanded along the same line, notwithstanding that you have given all the facts already. The time has come when the bureau would be well advised to co-ordinate these multifarious activities of the different departments.
There is another important point that must not be lost sight of. There is a head of one branch who has to do with the chemical and metallurgical industries, and he is an expensive official, and when you take into account the head of the Bureau of Statistics along with that staff you have an army of civil servants involving a tremendous overhead. I cannot emphasize too often the necessity for consolidating all this work under one administration, perhaps by the Bureau of Statistics. If this were done a good many positions could be abolished and a good deal of duplication of requests eliminated.
Is the census which is now taken merely a counting of noses, or does: it embrace all the details that are asked for in the decennial census?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I should like to meet my hon. friend's request, but I want some information in regard to these commissioners. We have a frank statement from the government that they are appointed not by the government but by western members or friends, I think the minister says. Of course, these western friends must be the representatives elected to this House from the west, or the defeated candidates who ran in the Liberal interests. Am I riglu or wrui..' in that assumption?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a pretty fair guess.

Will not the minister go further and say that I am right? The Minister of Public Work (Mr. King) says I am right, if I have heard him. Very well. I will put another question in connection with these gentlemen who are responsible for the appointments. Were any of them Progressives or were they all standpat Liberals?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: You will have to examine the list.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend would hardly expect me to pass by the Progressives.

I take it I am
right in that, Mr. Chairman. My hon. friend says I would not expect him to pass by the Progressives. I assume that means they also have had a share in the responsibility and in the honour and glory of getting their friends jobs on this work. Going a little further, did my hon. friend entirely overlook the claims

Supply-Trade and Commerce
of the Independents and was Labour's claim also overlooked in this patronage exploitation? Supposing we take the one lonely independent from British Columbia, surely he could not have been overlooked?
May I inform my hon. friend that no census is being taken in British Columbia this year?
May I ask my hon. friend how many Tories are seeking jobs?

My hon. friend's question is just as near the mark as might be expected; he is doing well. So we have these appointments made either on the recommendation of the sitting member, the defeated candidate or the Progressive gentleman who happens to be here. Under those circumstances, Mr Chairman. I think we should have information which will show the names of each one of those appointees and the name of the gentleman who appointed him. Then I think we would be able to apply his political colour, and to place the responsibility in the right quarter if we find that the appointment ought not to have been made. I would suggest to my hon. friend that he think that over and bring us down the list to-morrow.

The hon. gentleman having
raised the question he may as well get an answer. We do not want any patronage, and if it was offered we would not take it either from the Liberals or from the Conservatives.

I should like the minister seriously to consider the advisability of consolidating all the statistical branches in Ottawa. As a further evidence of my confidence in the Dominion Bureau of Statistics as presided oveir by the Chief Statistician, I am satisfied that if industry were only called upon by the Chief Statistician they would readily respond. But I have in mind what one of my Toronto colleagues referred to, the return that is made to three separate departments, the Income Tax department, the Labour department and the Bureau of Statistics. We shall soon come to an item of $100,000 for printing. We do not print nor do we compile these statistics for nothing, and in the final analysis it is simply a duplication of work. I believe the minister is anxious to economize, and I commend this to his attention as an opportunity for saving a very large sum of money.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me say again that I concur absolutely in what my hon. friend says, and I should like him to-morrow to give me the names of those three departments so I may check them back to the bureau.

Mr. Chairman, I understand
that the minister is going to furnish a list of the various census commissioners. Reference has already been made to the appointment of returned men to these positions. I am mainly concerned with their appointment, I do not care a rap what their politics may be. There is legislation providing that returned men, other things being equal, should get certain appointments. I see no reason in the world why in the case of census commissioners and enumerators the same rule should not prevail I think before this item passes the minister should let us have that list. I do not know why we should not also have a list of some of the more subordinate officials. I understand there is a commissioner for every electoral district, so the list would not be at all lengthy. I think we should be able to find out whether the appointees are returned men. I uo not say that in every case returned men were appointed in 1921, but if proper consideration was not given them the government of that day would have to take the responsibility, as the government of to-day will have to take it now. But I do think we ought to be able to get such a list before this item passes, and therefore I would ask the minister to allow it to stand until he brings down the list that he has already promised the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to make some
progress. I have already promised to bring down the list of 1921 and the last list. We may as well pass this item. I give my hon. friend my word that I will bring the list down.

I do not doubt the minister's word for one moment. I concur entirely in what has been said about his integrity. That is not my point at all. I submit we ought to have the list before the item passes, so that if we desire we may make some observations in connection with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I point out to my hon. friend that the civil government vote for this same department will afford him the opportunity he desires.
But, Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend will readily see that the vote under civil government cannot possibly cover the commissioners appointed under this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But I am undertaking to bring the list down.

But my hon. friend will see that under the circumstances there is no chance of discussing it. For example, we might have a little question as
1S52

Supply-Trade and Commerce
to the exact stripe of politics of some of the noble supporters of these gentlemen that have been appointed under this item. I would suggest that my hon. friend let this stand. We have had a pretty good discussion and now we only need the list. It may be perfectly innocuous, but at least it will be interesting.
And it would open up the question again in good shape.
Then what is my hon. friend afraid of?
Nothing, not even of the opposition.

Then I see nothing in his suggestion. Of course, he may be very much disappointed here because unfortunately owing to his geographical limitations he has had nothing to do with the list. Under the circumstances I would suggest that the committee rise and report progress.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like again to plead with my hon. friend. It is only half past ten and I think it is a fair compromise that we should pass this item and go home. I want to ask my hon. friend who is now leading the opposition (Sir Henry Drayton) and the gentleman who is sitting beside him, both of whom have had considerable experience in administration, how far it is going to get either party when I bring down the list of 1921 and the list of this year and my friends on both sides of the House debate their contents? Presumably it will open up a debate that will be neither very instructive nor very interesting. We might as well pass this item and adjourn.

We are not considering the vote of 1921; that list is not even in order for the purposes of a-may I use that word "bogey" again? Someone was angry because I used that word before. I crave the permission of the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) to use it again. The bogey of the list of 1921 is used for what purpose? It gives us something to consider, as to whether it will pay us to ask for this list as well. We have nothing to hide about the list of 1921.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And we have nothing to hide about this list.

As it is used in that way, Mr. Chairman, I insist the more strongly upon the production of that list. We will take full responsibility for everything that happened in 1921. Those appointments were criticised; there was a great deal of talk
TSir Henry Drayton.J
when those lists of 1921 were being considered, with charges of patronage levelled against us, and we have gone through it all. Now it is the turn of my hon. friends. It is their vote, and it is something which has to do particularly with their vote. It has so much to do with it that my. hon. friend the minister undertakes to produce it, but it cannot be properly discussed with the item closed.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

I think I had the floor before the minister made his motion. I wanted to ask on this item if the minister, when he sent to his friends in the prairie provinces requests for recommendations for appointments in connection with this census, pointed out that a desirable qualification for the position was that of being a returned man?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have the qualifications which were given me by the census enumerator. I have not them here; they are in my desk.

I only wanted to bring this to the attention of the minister.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
